strings.name: Wole Soyinka
strings.summary: Soyinka grew up in Nigeria and studied in Britain before combining Yoruba traditions with modern drama. His work examines colonial legacies, power and individual responsibility. Imprisoned during the civil war, he continued writing plays, poetry, fiction and public commentary. In 1986 he became the first African writer awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. His artistic practice has intertwined with opposition to political repression.

strings.influence.rationale: Through drama, poetry and public writing, he connects Yoruba culture with modern politics and is the first African writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.f2.label: Education
strings.facts.f2.value: University College Ibadan; BA with honours in English, University of Leeds (1957)
strings.highlights.h1.title: Yoruba traditions and modern drama
strings.highlights.h1.text: Works including Death and the King’s Horseman examine ritual, power and cultural encounters.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Nobel Prize in Literature
strings.highlights.h2.text: Awarded the prize in 1986, becoming its first African literary laureate.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Discusses US visa revocation
strings.timeline.t1.text: Publicly said in Lagos that the United States had revoked his non-immigrant visa; the statement is attributed to him.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Returns to the novel
strings.timeline.t2.text: Published Chronicles from the Land of the Happiest People on Earth, satirizing personal and political corruption in an imaginary Nigeria.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Receives the Nobel Prize in Literature
strings.timeline.t3.text: The Swedish Academy recognized drama with a broad cultural perspective, bringing renewed international attention to African literature.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Publishes a major play
strings.timeline.t4.text: Death and the King’s Horseman brought Yoruba ritual and conflict under colonial rule into drama.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Imprisoned during the civil war
strings.timeline.t5.text: Arrested after efforts to avert Nigeria’s civil war, he endured prolonged solitary confinement before release in 1969.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Returns to theatre in Nigeria
strings.timeline.t6.text: Returned to Nigeria and formed a theatre company; A Dance of the Forests was associated with cultural events around independence.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Completes studies at Leeds
strings.timeline.t7.text: Earned an honours degree in English at Leeds, then worked with London’s Royal Court Theatre.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Born in Abeokuta
strings.timeline.t8.text: Grew up in a Yoruba family, with Christian education and local cultural traditions shaping his early surroundings.
